evidence: TaskService.createTask orchestrates: checks the project exists via getProject, checks the user exists via users.existsById, builds a Task and calls tasks.save, then returns toDto(task). This is use-case coordination.
TaskService.markTaskDone hands the state change to the domain entity (task.markDone()) and then saves it through the TaskRepository interface.
requireText and parseDueDate check input at the boundary and throw the application-level InvalidInputError. They contain no HTTP status codes or framework types.
toDto maps a Task entity to the TaskDto contract (dueDate?.toISOString()). Mapping to DTOs is an application-layer job.
The file has no persistence code (SQL, file or DB clients) and no transport or framework code (request/response objects, routing).
parsedVerdict.reasoning: src/application/task-service.ts does work that belongs in an application layer. TaskService coordinates use cases: it creates projects, users and tasks, lists tasks and marks a task done. It works only through repository interfaces defined in the domain layer and an injected ID generator. Its other jobs are checking input at the boundary (required text, parsing the due date, checking the status value), raising application-level errors (ResourceNotFoundError, InvalidInputError) and mapping entities to DTOs (toDto). The file contains no persistence code: no SQL, no storage clients and no in-memory store. It also has no transport or framework logic, such as HTTP request or response handling, status codes or routing. Behaviour that changes state is left to the domain (task.markDone()). A few things sit near the line but are normal for an application service: the default status 'todo' and the check against taskStatuses are a use-case default and boundary validation, and checking that an assignee exists is cross-aggregate coordination. None of these is a domain invariant taken over from the entity.
